utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. If the witness could be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, once again. And I remind you again of the affirmation. Yes, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Rodic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Jokic. Yesterday, among other things, we talked about 11 points, or rather, the proposal to normalise life in Dubrovnik and provide security for the town of Dubrovnik. Did you take part in any of these negotiations with the Dubrovnik side and the Monitoring Mission of the EC?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that on several occasions?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I took part on the 10th of October, together with General Ruzinovski, in Meljine. Then on the same day, on a warship called Kotor; and on the 28th of October with General Strugar in Meljine. Then on the 5th of December, when the cease-fire agreement was brokered in Cavtat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the month of November 1991, were you perhaps present at the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me remind you, in November I think Mr. Kouchner also came. Were there any talks held then?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In November, we organised entering Mokosica, a neighbourhood in Rijeka Dubrovacka and the hand-over of weapons. Negotiations were then held by General Damjanovic on behalf of the command of the 2nd Operational Group. On that occasion, before entering Mokosica, I met Mr. Kouchner, and we entered Mokosica together. However, I was not involved in any negotiations. Even before that, General Strugar strictly decided who would be involved in the negotiations. I think there were some problems there with Colonel Svicevic, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, did you agree with this proposal of 11 points, as it was compiled, in favour of the peaceful settlement of the situation around Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, of course, with its very essence. I agreed with the very essence of these proposals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since the Supreme Command had set the objectives and issued tasks to the 2nd Operational Group for the operations that it was supposed to carry out, did the Supreme Command also participate in the proposals of -- for the normalisation of life in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Probably it was the Supreme Command that provided the basis for that proposal. I don't know exactly, but that is normal procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the usher to distribute a document, if possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the same document that we had occasion to see already. However, I have not seen this authentic document. I saw the one that everybody received.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're talking about --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The proposal for normalisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The proposal for normalisation that was admitted into evidence as a Prosecution exhibit that you looked at during the examination-in-chief. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us where the two documents differ. Are these 11 points identical in both documents?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the points are identical to that proposal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, in the introduction to the document, a difference can be seen. Can you explain this to us? This document was addressed to the operational centre of the General Staff of the armed forces of the SFRY. These are proposals that were sent along with a short letter. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the introduction, it says that in agreement with the head of the first administration, Lieutenant Colonel General Simonovic, the text of the proposal was drafted, and was submitted to the members of the mission of the European Community and the representatives of the town of Dubrovnik. The deadline for responding to these proposals is the 27th of October 1991 until 2000 hours. That's the only difference.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that, as we said, the Supreme Command actively participated in everything concerning the situation in Dubrovnik, including these proposals to normalise life there; that is to say, this offer for a peaceful solution and for disarming the paramilitaries? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this document also show that the Supreme Command was informed about everything in relation to these proposals and that it took part in their creation?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that can be seen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to ask that this document be assigned a number and be admitted into evidence as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document is D52.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the usher for his assistance regarding the next document.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this a document that the command of the 9th VPS is sending to its subordinate units, which was received on the 4th of November by the command of the 472nd Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Inter alia, we see that this document is entitled "Information About Activities and the State of Morale in the Units," and it is addressed to Trebinje, Prevlaka and Radovici, the commanders of those barracks. Can you tell us these localities where the barracks are? Where do they belong, bearing in mind republican boundaries?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Radovici barracks is on the peninsula of Ljustica and Montenegro. The barracks of Prevlaka is in the Republic of Croatia; and Trebinje is in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the beginning of this document, it says that on the 3rd of November, members of the paramilitary formation of Croatia opened fire at 1750 hours from the area of Petka against the JNA units. Is that part of the information that we discussed yesterday, of that report that was sent to Admiral Brovet?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is contained in that information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It says further on: "According to the information we have within the ramparts of the Old Town, there are about 800 mercenaries stationed." Did you receive information through intelligence reports or in other ways about the deployment of the enemy?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note that they do not have the document. Could it please be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what information this is, that 800 black shirts were stationed within the ramparts.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, there has been no predicate laid as to whether or not the witness even has familiarity with this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I did ask the witness Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. about the document in the first place, and he identified it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: He identified it as a document, but not one of which he had any knowledge. If you're wanting to search about his knowledge, he hasn't, at the moment, indicated he has any.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, would it be sufficient on page 4 in line 22, in response to my question related to this document, there is an answer provided by the witness. Would that do?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What does it say?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may be of assistance, in response to the question of the Defence counsel: [In English] "Is this a document that the command of the 9th VPS is sending to its subordinate units, which was received on the 4th November by the command of the Motorised Brigade?" [Interpretation] In response to that question, the witness answers: "Yes, that's right." We believe that this is sufficient foundation in terms of the witness's position vis a vis this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, that answer is merely identifying the document on its face. That's what the document appears to be, and that information is apparently what it is saying on the face of the document. Now, if you're wanting to know from this witness whether what is in here is true or this was actually a report received and so on, at the moment he has not indicated that he himself has any knowledge of the document or its content. Am I ahead of you, Ms. Somers, or at least up with you?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Right there with me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this a document of your command?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can explain, though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is information, a paper, that my assistant for political work is sending to the command. He has the right to do so. And every day, or when necessary, he sends information on his own to subordinate units. I do not review that, and there's no need for me to do it. That is why I had not seen this document. Otherwise, I primarily agree with everything that is written in this document, except for this particular statement, and I don't know where it comes from; namely, that 800 Croatian members of the forces could have been within the ramparts of the Old Town. That is my only objection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me who made up the command of the 9th VPS, meaning the officers, and can you give us their names and their individual positions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me. That was asked and answered, Your Honour, in examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: My recollection is not that good. But is yours any better, Mr. Rodic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would kindly ask my learned friend not to interrupt me all the time. Had she listened to my question, it would have been quite clear that it does not pertain only to the signatory of this document. I asked for all the names and positions of the members of his command, all of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: With respect, Your Honour, that is exactly what I was referring to. But if the Chamber wishes to hear repetition, then...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, it's so long ago, Ms. Somers, that it has passed from my instant clear recall. It won't hurt to have a revision.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you asking as of the date of this letter, 3rd of November?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. But that situation goes beyond the 3rd of November. It pertains to the period from October through December 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please go ahead, Mr. Jokic.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. I shall say the following: At the beginning of the operation and towards the end, as I was about to leave, the situation had not changed in respect of the actual composition of my command. The chief of staff was Captain Milan Zec, Battleship Captain Milan Zec. The chief of operations was Slobodan Kozaric, Frigate Captain. The assistant for moral and political affairs was Frigate Captain Zarkovic, Mihajlo Zarkovic. The assistant commander for logistics was Colonel Petar Dragicevic. The assistant chief of staff for intelligence affairs was Frigate Captain Sofronije Jeremic. Of course, this includes the chiefs of arms and services who represent the staff of the sector but who are not directly subordinated to me. They are directly subordinated to the chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. All these assistants that you listed, did they work autonomously, independently, or within the frameworks of the staff and command of the 9th VPS?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they worked within the frameworks of the staff and command. And my assistants had some independent authorisations as well, as we were able to see from this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When it comes to this piece of information about the 800 mercenaries and black shirts stationed within the walls of the Old Town, would your assistant, for example, think up such a thing, construe it and invent it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The contents of this information should have been drawn by him from the work of the staff, the intelligence and information from the operations centre and intelligence data generally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the possibility exist that from intelligence gained, he had information that at a certain point in time this number of enemy forces were actually stationed in the Old Town? Could he have had that kind of information?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot believe that that was possible because it wasn't the information I had at that time, that there were such -- there was such a large number of these men stationed in the walls, in the ramparts of the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you think? What led him to present this piece of information?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he exaggerated too much or gave his own free interpretation of some unreliable intelligence gathered. And at the time, there was quite a lot of this going on, unreliable intelligence. And I can give you examples, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, this document plus the information, would it go down to the lower units, the subordinated units within the command?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Among other things, was it designed to warn and caution when enemy information is supplied?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the one-but-last sentence of that first paragraph, it says from the naval vessels, there was strong retaliation, a strong response. Now, if you look at the first sentence describing the action against the JNA, would that follow on?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your engineers units, did they have a lot of work in that Dubrovnik area?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did. There were a lot of mines that had been planted and areas that had to be de-mined to establish communication along the coastal roads and so on, and in the settlements and approach roads.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the members of the JNA suffer any losses in terms of men and technical equipment due to the mines laid on the roads and other areas, other booby traps and so on?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We did suffer losses and casualties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this document, it is stated that already on the 3rd of November Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the commands in Cavtat, Grud, Srebrno, and Zupa fulfilled the assignments given them which led to -- which were in line with the normalisation of life in those places. Was that something that was done on a daily basis and a daily effort?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. We wanted to have the population return from Dubrovnik and Cavtat where they had fled due to the combat operations going on. We wanted the population to come back so that they could continue to till the land and go about their farming on their land and in their households.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, at the end of this document, does the assistant commander issue tasks to all subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, he does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And does this end by saying that the -- everybody must be informed with information contained in this document?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I should like to tender this document into evidence. May it be assigned a number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document is D53.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I have the usher's assistance, please, for the next document to be distributed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to point out that there's no command level or anything listed on this document from the sender.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with the Court's permission, we shall explain the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, have you had enough time to look through the document?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know -- are the contents of this document familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: -- the question is is the document familiar, not just the contents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think a lot of these matters, Ms. Somers, will sort themselves out if left for a moment or two.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I am familiar with a portion of these contents, especially this piece of information which relates to the sabotage units that stormed the combat positions of the 1st Company of the 1st Battalion of the 472nd Brigade because that is what was contained in the report and piece of information that we wrote and addressed to Admiral Brovet.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't seen this document before. None of the documents of the 472nd Brigade are ones that I have seen in the military archives. Those documents suddenly disappeared in an unexplained way, and I wasn't able to access them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me something else now, please: This document in its left-hand corner at the top, it says "highly confidential, number 11-187/28," and the date is 06/11/1991. And the signature is, the issuer of this document, and it says "Assistant commander for moral guidance and legal affairs, Captain of the frigate." Now, on this copy, what we're lacking - that is true - is the name and surname. We cannot see, just like on the previous document, the one that was tendered and admitted a moment ago dated the 3rd of November, we see the command of the 9th VPS there. Regardless of these shortcomings in this document, would you say that the overall document, by virtue of its contents and appearance and stamp having been received by the 472nd Motorised Brigade, represents a document of the 9th VPS? Would you say that was one of its documents?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. There has been evidence by this witness that he has never seen documents of the 472nd Brigade and he cannot answer this question. And further, he has indicated recognising only part of the document -- contents, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I should once again like to ask that you prevail so that my learned colleague of the Prosecution can hear me out, hear my questions out and the witness's answers. He never claimed that this was a document of the 472nd Motorised Brigade, but that it was from the archives of the 472nd Brigade. So the witness did not actually say that this document was issued by the 472nd Brigade itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Rodic, I cannot agree with you. The witness has indicated he doesn't know what is the source of this document. He has no knowledge, was his evidence, of the records of the 472nd Brigade, and he has not indicated any personal knowledge of any part of the document. He did recognise that the content of it dealt with the subject matter with which he was familiar in one respect only but not to say that he knew this document in that respect. So at the moment, this document is something which is in no way identified by this witness. So I think you're at a dead end on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, can you tell us whether this is the document of your assistant for moral guidance and legal affairs? That is to say, Frigate Captain Mihajlo Zarkovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. The same objection stands. The witness does not know where the document emanated from. He has been handed a document he does not recognise, and I think counsel is not accepting the Chamber's ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Nor are you allowing the witness to answer a quite different question. Admiral, of your personal knowledge, do you know the author of this document, or do you just not recognise the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my opinion is that this is a document by Frigate Captain Mihajlo Zarkovic, judging by the way in which it was compiled. It is similar to the way he would have written it. So I would say that that was it. But as I say, I have never seen the document before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think that's about the high-water mark you're going to reach, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I take a moment, or rather could the witness be handed Prosecution Exhibit P116, from tab 16, with the usher's assistance, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, would you compare these two documents, please. You're an experienced professional with respect to military correspondence. And tell me, please, where the difference lies between these two documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Did you say tab 16, Exhibit P116?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I see remarkably different documents. Have you got the right one?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The document I asked the witness to be given is an order by the chief of the General Staff. "Order from the chief of the General Staff" is the title of the document. And I would like to compare the form of the two documents and have the witness give us his opinion about that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that it is difficult to compare these two documents because one was written by the assistant for political affairs, and the second document is by the chief of the General Staff. However, there are certain similarities when it comes to the last paragraph in both these documents, and that is the form and shape of documents generally sent out as pieces of information, documents designed to inform the -- all the men and forces down the chain of command and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you another question. This is an order from the chief of the General Staff, this particular document. Have you ever seen it written in this form? So I'm not talking about the contents now, just visually, the form of the document, have you ever seen it compiled in this way; the title, the heading, and so on? What a document of this kind should have in its upper left-hand corner, the numbers, the date of the document, order, et cetera, signature, and so on and so forth, things like that, the general aspect of the document in an order from the chief of the General Staff of the armed forces of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Was this the kind of military document issued by the army and written by the army when it wrote a document like this? I'm not talking about contents, just the form and general aspect.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, well, we didn't quite understand each other. As far as form is concerned, this document of the chief of the General Staff does not have the form of a military document. It was extracted from some publication or book, because it says "Attachment 102."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When answering the questions put by my learned friend of the Prosecution during the examination-in-chief about this document, you said that you had not seen it before but that you were familiar with its contents. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, along those lines, yes. Well, I still think so. That is what I still think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, this document, this other document that you have in front of you, the information about the activities and the state of morale in units, does it correspond to the appropriate form of writing documents in military units?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does. However, in the upper left-hand corner, there is no mention of the command that is sending the document; and down at the bottom, there is no name and surname of the person who compiled the document. The rest is fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the basis of your experience, when you look at the way in which this was typed out, or rather if you look at the actual lettering on this document, is this a teleprinter, a typewriter, or something else? Can you assist us with that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is a typewriter. But I know the style or -- well, perhaps that's a better word, of the assistant for political activity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this document, do you recognise his style?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what I just said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just wanted to ask you, if it's not too much of a problem, to do it again, once again.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already said that this is how he writes. When his papers are compared, then his last and one-but-last paragraphs tend to be like this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You said that you were familiar with this incident that had been reported earlier, that a sabotage group of the enemy was prevented from entering the troops of the 9th VPS. And do you know that fire was opened, artillery fire was opened, at your units on that day?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what it says here. Of course I cannot remember now. He probably took this information from the operative centre, but of course I don't remember, except for this sabotage group, but I don't remember the rest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had your units been targeted by artillery fire, as it says here, Dubac, Brgat, Zarkovica? Would the superior command have to be notified then as to where the fire was coming from, how many shells fell on them, the kind of fire that is opened at them? Is the superior command informed about such things?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is their duty to inform the superior command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The information about these reports of subordinate units, are they logged in some records at the operations centre, this content of what the subordinate units have to report?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All orders, all reports are entered into the war logbook hour by hour, and that is recorded by the operations centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The assistant commander for moral guidance and political affairs, Mihajlo Zarkovic, does he have access to this information, such information?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore, in this case, does he provide information that 51 shells fell on one place, 63 on another place on that particular day, the 6th of November?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what's written here. He probably copied that from the information received in the operations centre. That would be the normal procedure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you happen to know, do you happen to remember this situation of the 7th of November, that a meeting was supposed to be held between the representatives of the Red Cross of Herceg-Novi, Trebinje, Dubrovnik, at the request of the people of Dubrovnik, in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that, but I do know that they had meetings. I know that they had meetings, the representatives of the Red Cross. Several times, at that. And this piece of information is certainly right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Frigate Captain Zarkovic, does he say that JNA units responded by fire after the enemy took action only after they had previously informed the members of the EC Mission about this?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what's written here, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to object to the question and ask the answer be stricken. There's no indication that Zarkovic, in fact, said anything. He said the writing is similar to Zarkovic. The Prosecution would object to any conclusion drawn by counsel that it was actually Zarkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You're once again, Mr. Rodic, trying to strain this for everything you can and going too far. This document hasn't been identified as the document of any witness. I see it at the moment as no higher than "apparently" issued by the assistant commander for moral and political affairs and as to which the present witness is not able to verify the accuracy or reliability of any of the contents. Now, what you have been asking is a series of questions, the effect of which is "Is this what the document says"? If you're doing that with the object of proving the truth of that, you haven't got there. I think you'll have to find some other way, and not this document, to get there with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour. I'm not going to pursue the matter further, this particular document. But the designation that is missing in the document of my learned friend, namely the number of the document, et cetera, that is missing, I'm going to try to provide that. But could this document now please be assigned a number and admitted?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: We object to any assignment, even for identification, and for admission. The document has no reliability, and has not been authenticated in any way by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber will receive the document. We fully appreciate the reason for Ms. Somers' objection and the substance that lies underneath that reason and we see the document as no higher than I have indicated to Mr. Rodic. It is "apparently" a document of that description. Its contents will not stand as proof of them but it will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document is marked D55. Excuse me, D54.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask that the witness be shown a Prosecution exhibit, P136 from tab 34.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I gave the elements for the content of this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Only elements for the content. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was not present when it was sent. If that is what you meant. I was not present when it was sent, but --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You were not present when the document was sent. But what I'm interested in specifically is each and every sentence of this document. Did you write each and every sentence of this document? Could you please just wait for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We have a problem at the moment in the transcript, Mr. Rodic. Your question at line 17 was not received and interpreted.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I asked the witness whether he wrote this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rodic. That will clarify the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, I would like to ask you the following now: Would you tell me whether you wrote each and every sentence of this document yourself? Of the content, I mean; that's what I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've told you that I gave the elements for sending such a telegram with this content. And now whether I wrote every word or every sentence, I probably did not because I'm not a writing clerk, I'm not a scribe. I dictated what the telegram was supposed to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we look at this document, everything that we can read in it, was it dictated by you yourself?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the bottom of this message sent to the minister, Mr. Rudolf, it says that it was received on the 6th of December at approximately 1400 hours. Were you in Kumbor or Kupari at that time when this message was received in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not there then. I was en route to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you happen to remember when you dictated the contents of this message?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's too difficult for me to answer that after 13 years. Do you want the minute or what?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, you were asked a number of times during many interviews about that, and I'm not asking you for the minute, of course. I'm asking you for a rough estimate of the time when you dictated the contents of this message.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before my departure to Podgorica by helicopter. That means sometime between 12.00, half past 12.00, quarter to 1.00 perhaps at the latest. That's when this could have been done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember where you were when you dictated the contents of this message?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Cavtat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who you dictated the contents of the message to?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The message was for the chief of staff, and I dictated it at the Cavtat headquarters, to Colonel Dulija -- or rather, he was Captain Nemanja Kurdulija at the time, I think. Anyway, this was a paper that was to be handed to the chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, Captain Kurdulija in Cavtat took down the contents of the message which you dictated to him, and the message was to have been sent to your chief of staff, Milan Zec. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you happen to know whether Kurdulija conveyed the message on, your message, to the chief of staff Mr. Zec; how, in what way, if so, if he did send it on to Mr. Zec?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the details. I think Zec arrived and took the message himself and sent it on via fax to Dubrovnik. I think that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see Zec on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. I'm not quite sure, though. We did talk over the phone. But I don't think we actually saw each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From this, it would emerge that Zec went to Cavtat and that from Cavtat he faxed the message on to Dubrovnik. Would that be what happened?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can't say that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The answer, Mr. Rodic, has confirmed the accuracy of Ms. Somers' objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where the message was sent on from to Minister Rudolf by the JNA? Was it Cavtat, Kupari, or Kumbor?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't know that. I was en route to Belgrade so of course, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you know it was faxed?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. I think that can be seen from this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Judging by the contents of this message, the third sentence reads: "General Kadijevic sent you a message, and the ECMM - the European Monitoring Mission - in Dubrovnik, on undertaking an energetic investigation on our responsibility and the guilty ones for this event...," as the message reads. Can you tell me when you learned that General Kadijevic had sent a message to Minister Rudolf and the ECMM Monitoring Mission?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the morning of that day, around 7.00 a.m., when the command of the 2nd Operational Group called me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what did the command of the 2nd Operational Group tell you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me that General Kadijevic called him and said that he was informed about the attack on the town, on Dubrovnik, and that the attack should be stopped, who the perpetrators of the attack were should be ascertained, and an investigation conducted, and to inform Dubrovnik -- or rather, to link up with Dubrovnik - I don't know what he actually said; I'm giving a free interpretation - liaise with the people of Dubrovnik and stop the attack. And then he said that he would undertake an investigation to seek out the culprits and request that they, for their part, establish who the culprits were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "they," do you mean General Kadijevic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know when General Kadijevic sent a message to Minister Rudolf and the European Community Monitoring Mission? Give us a time frame, if you can.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. Everything I knew at the time was what I've already told you. Of course, it went on for longer -- for longer. But I don't know when he talked to them, when General Kadijevic talked to Minister Rudolf. And I don't know whether he sent a message of some kind after that conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were you able to write the contents of this message in this way, then?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wrote what I wrote. What General Strugar told me, that's what I put inside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By noon, by 12.00 noon, let's say, roughly speaking, is it true that you had no contact with General Kadijevic at all by that time? And I'm thinking of the 6th of December 1991.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I know that they were -- he was looking for me and the chief of the General Staff as well but we never actually spoke.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did General Kadijevic and the chief of the General Staff, Blagoje Adzic, look for you? Where did they try to reach you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know where they tried to reach me. But from my talk with General Strugar, I understood that they were trying to reach me over the phone. I don't know where they tried to reach me. But when I returned from Belgrade, I heard from Admiral Kandic that they had tried to reach me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was General Kandic himself at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was on the island of Vis, at his command post.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the command post of the Military Naval District; is that it? Did they then try via Admiral Kandic to find you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. The chief of the General Staff, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the following sentence, you go on to say the following: "At the same time, we expect to find out the responsibilities on your side for the sake of a further clarification of all circumstances in regard with the events of last night and this morning." So are you, in fact, asking that responsibility be established on the other side as well for these events that took place on the 6th of December 1991?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any reason for establishing the other side's responsibility for this?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was reason. I was informed by the duty operations officer and the chief of the operational department that they had opened fire from the Dubrovnik side, targeting the units of the 3rd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you ever receive an answer from the opposite side with respect to your request that they look into who was responsible within their own units?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not a written response. I never received a written answer. All I received was an oral answer on that day, at around 10.00, a little before 10.00. Rather, between 9.00 and 10.00, when I talked to the minister, Minister Rudolf, and the next day, on the 7th during the negotiations of agreeing upon a truce, a cease-fire. And both times, he claimed that from the Dubrovnik side, as far as he knew, there was no opening of fire as a reason or motive, as he said, for launching an attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know whether the other side, the opposite side, that is to say, the Croatian side, investigated their own possible responsibility for that, the responsibility of their units for launching into provocations on their side?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't know that, of course. But from the answer I was given, it became clear that they did not do that. And the commander, the defence commander, never mentioned that at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time, Mr. Rodic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, before the break, you said to me that you did not know whether the Croat side had investigated who was responsible for the provocations coming from their side. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the two conversations you mentioned that you had with Minister Rudolf, did you conclude on the basis of these conversations that they never conducted an investigation at all?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it could be put that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell me, on the 6th of December, as this event was taking place, or on the 7th of December when you were at the negotiations in Cavtat, or perhaps on the 8th of December when the officers of the 9th VPS were recording the damage incurred in Dubrovnik, did you ever ask the other side to have a joint investigation carried out, ever?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to look at item 4 in this letter. In this letter, where you address Minister Rudolf, you apologise to him for the impossibility to attend the negotiations on the 6th of December. But you suggest the following as regards the continuation of negotiations. There are eight points mentioned here in terms of an agreement between the JNA and the Croatian side. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 4, do you propose that ships be controlled in the harbour of Gruz?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this supposed to be ships that are supposed to navigate into Dubrovnik or from Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those are the ships that are meant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When one says "control of ships," does that mean that these checks should be conducted by members of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in paragraph 7, within the proposal to have a total deblockade of Dubrovnik, is it proposed that the armaments that are a threat to town be withdrawn and that armed men that came to town should be evacuated on the first vessels that leave?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The essence of this proposal is to deblock the town from land and sea, but the ships sailing into town should be checked. This problem of armed personnel which could not have been resolved in a satisfactory manner, because they did not accept disarmament and a surrender of weapons, so this could have been a solution. The proposal was aimed at having these armed volunteers leave town with their arms on the first vessels that will sail out of town, that that should be stated, established, and that both sides should thus be satisfied. That's the core of the issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, is it correct that in the agreement between the Croatian side and the JNA that was signed on the 7th of December, which you signed on behalf of the Supreme Command of the JNA, it was also agreed that ships be checked in the harbour of Gruz?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what you suggested on the 6th of December under paragraph 4 was adopted on the 7th of December; and in the agreement of the 7th of December, it was accepted that ships would be checked in the port of Gruz. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, how far away is Cavtat from Kupari?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Kupari? About 3 to 4 -- or rather 3 to 5 miles. By sea.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about by land?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By land? Well, about 20 kilometres, between 15 and 20 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, on that morning of the 6th of December, at a given point in time, you arrived in Cavtat from Kumbor, and you stayed in Cavtat until you left for Belgrade on the 6th of December. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far away is Cilipi airport from Cavtat?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, between 8 to 10 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, while you were in Cavtat on the 6th of December, were you at the command all the time? At the JNA command for the town of Cavtat? Were you with Captain Kurdulija at Captain Kurdulija's office?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, does that mean that you spent all this time in his office?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, as for means of communication, what was there in that office?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what all the things in that office were. This was the office of Atlas, a travel agency, a Dubrovnik travel agency, Atlas. And there were civilian links to Dubrovnik from there. What else was there by means of communications equipment, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's try to deal with it this way: Did the telephone in that office work? So were you able to communicate with Dubrovnik, with the forward command post in Kupari, with Kumbor?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Captain Kurdulija have radio communication equipment in that office and, therefore, communication with the forward command post in Kupari or with Kumbor or other JNA units?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he had radio relay links. I'm not sure that he had a radio link. Perhaps he had a Motorola, but I doubt it. He didn't need one anyway. He had radio relay links, and also there was the civilian line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to us the difference between radio relay links and Motorolas or radio communications, as you refer to them, in respect of communication as such.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a Motorola is a radio transmitter at a very high frequency, the so-called VVF. And it can be used for communication with another party that has this same kind of frequency and the same kind of equipment. As far as radio relay communications are concerned, it is a type of communication involving a conversation by telephone but not by wire. The two parties speaking do so through a radio relay. At that time, the lines between Kumbor, Cavtat, and Kupari were wire lines, and they had been destroyed. So the basic means of communication was radio relay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, this radio relay, was it a military radio relay communication, a military communication as such?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these were military communications.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, which units in the field could use this radio relay communication?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commands could use it, certain commands of units where these communication links had been set up; that is to say, stationary commands. Or radio vehicles could be used involving types of equipment that could be used by a certain level of command. For example, a brigade had that type of communications but battalions did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In order to have a radio relay communication, is it necessary to have some kind of equipment? If so, what type of equipment?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, it does require equipment. I already said it means that there has to be a radio vehicle where the appropriate equipment is mounted. There is different kinds of equipment involved. I'm not a signalsman, a communications officer myself. I hope you're not asking me for the actual type of equipment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Don't worry. I know that you're not a signalsman, but I'm a layperson myself to a considerable extent so I'm asking you about it because I believe that you do have more knowledge about it after all. And this radio vehicle that you mentioned, so in addition to an automobile where this radio link can be, can this kind of radio link be in a particular facility, like at a command post of a military unit? So can it be in a stationary facility, this kind of radio link?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. Well, these communications are set up as a type of communication in stationary headquarters, and also in radio vehicles for units that are on the move.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So apart from these two types of communication, namely, radio relay and radio communications via a Motorola, which we mentioned until now, did the military in that area have its own wire communication lines, if that includes a field telephone or things like that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were wire communication lines for all units at lower levels, like battalions, commands of particular villages or towns, many checkpoints of the military police, guard posts. Or rather, more important guard posts had wire communication links. And it was the line units that placed the lines there when necessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "line units," I assume that these are units of the JNA belonging to the signals service which make it possible for contact to be established by wire between and among units. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, on the 6th of December when you moved from Kumbor to Cavtat and in the area, did you have a vehicle made available to you? If so, what kind of vehicle and who drove you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had a military vehicle, a Puch military vehicle, which I invariably took. I did not have another vehicle. I did not use another vehicle. I had a driver, and I had two escorts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your driver a soldier who was doing his military service, or was it a professional driver? When I say "professional," was this a civilian who was employed by the JNA? Or was it a regular soldier doing his military service?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a regular soldier doing his military service. At first, for a while, I had a driver who was a professional, a civilian who had been mobilised. But that was only at the very beginning, I think for the first 20-odd days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that soldier drive you on the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember what his name was?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. If I were to hear it, I would probably recognise it, but he was a Montenegrin, somewhere from around Podgorica. And the man who accompanied me was called Sainovic, and he was from Bar, my escort.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This escort, Sainovic, was he a regular soldier, or was he an officer, a professional?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were all regular soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where the other escort was from and what his name was?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember him. One was from Herceg-Novi; I remember that. But they would replace each other because the security service would assign them as security details and replace them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me please, from Cilipi -- or rather, on the 6th of December, did you fly to Podgorica from Cilipi airport?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you fly by helicopter?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, a helicopter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know whether the helicopter was from a unit from Mostar, from the Mostar airport? Is that where it belonged? Or was it part of a unit located at the airport Golubovci in Podgorica?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I didn't know the people. I didn't know those men because I didn't usually fly by helicopter. I don't know whether that was the only time during that period of time that I flew by helicopter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, how much time is needed to fly from Cilipi airport to the airport in Podgorica?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, with takeoff and landing, it lasts about 20 minutes to half an hour, all things considered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived in Podgorica on the 6th of December, did you take off for Belgrade straight away, or did you have a brief delay or a short stay there?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, we took off straight away because we were running a little late anyway, I think. And General Strugar was already waiting. As far as my memory serves me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember where General Strugar was waiting for you, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember. I think it was at the airport, at the airport command, Golubovci. I think, but I'm not sure. I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, fine. Now, do you perhaps remember which plane you flew to Belgrade in?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I really don't remember. It might have been a JAK-40, but I'm not sure. It wasn't the French aircraft. I do know that, the one that we otherwise had. I don't remember any salon on board or anything of that kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, tell me, this JAK-40 aircraft, how long does it take to fly the distance from Podgorica to Belgrade? How long was the flight?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think about 45 minutes, an hour with the arrival from the airport, from the military airport. To the airport itself, perhaps 45 minutes, thereabouts. Maybe more; 50 minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, did you land at the Batajnica military airport at Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Batajnica I think it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you then from Batajnica airport -- were you driven from the airport in a vehicle when you went to see General Kadijevic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And roughly how much time did that take? How much does it take to drive from Batajnica airport to the Federal Secretariat for National Defence in Belgrade, which was where General Kadijevic was?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, half an hour perhaps, 20 minutes to half an hour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you happen to remember whether the federal secretary received you immediately upon your arrival, or did you have to wait?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't remember having had to wait at all. I just remember that when we went in, they were there. That is to say, the generals who were supposed to be there. That's what I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now, can you tell me, please, time-wise how long you stayed at the meeting with General Kadijevic, talking to him.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the conversation lasted about an hour, roughly speaking. It was just the two of us that talked. So it was a dialogue between the two of us. Nobody else spoke or interrupted. I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after the conversation with the federal secretary, did you perhaps go to see someone else? Did you see to some other business at the General Staff building perhaps?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't remember having done so. As far as I recall, we returned after that conversation. We went back to the plane.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you take the same route back; that is to say, were you driven to Batajnica airport and then flew from Batajnica airport to Podgorica?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I think so, at least, as far as I remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, when you arrived at Podgorica, did you and General Strugar go further on together? What happened next upon your arrival in Podgorica?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we went together. We were driven in the same vehicle to Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which vehicle was that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. How can I remember something like that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how much time does it take, driven in a vehicle, to get from the airport at Podgorica to, I suppose, the command post at Trebinje where you were heading for?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think about an hour, it would take you about an hour. But I'm not sure. If you go by Niksic, perhaps an hour, hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you stop off at Trebinje at the command post of the 2nd Operational Group perhaps?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay there, roughly?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how long we stayed. But I think we talked and discussed our next steps, steps over the next few days, the assignments and tasks we had. So that must have been at least half an hour then. We looked at a report there, I assume, from the 3rd Battalion. I think the 3rd Battalion was already there. So we discussed the negotiations to be held the following day, the press conference, and dispatching officers to investigate the damages in Dubrovnik, to record the damages in Dubrovnik, as well as something about Captain Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, from Trebinje, where did you go from there? And we're still speaking about the 6th of December; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. From Trebinje, I went to Kupari.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go to Kupari by car?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think so, yes. What else? How else?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how far is the drive from Trebinje to Kupari, roughly speaking? How long does it take?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Half an hour. A little less, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You reached Kupari at the forward command post of the 9th VPS, I assume. That's where you went?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know perhaps in kilometres what the distance is from Podgorica to Trebinje?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I really can't say. Perhaps about, if you go via Niksic, 100 to 120 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you happen to remember when from Cilipi airport you left for Podgorica -- or rather Belgrade, on the 6th of December? The time, when was that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was about 12.30. Perhaps a little later. I could be wrong, give or take half an hour to an hour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you remember when I asked about the contents of the message sent to the minister, Minister Rudolf, you said that you dictated the contents of that message between 12.00 and 12.45. Does that mean that you left after that, that you left for Cilipi in the helicopter after that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it means between 12.00 and 12.45. That's what it means. I can't be certain 14 years on when I left, the exact time I left to board that flight. So there's always plus/minus possibilities of up to half an hour. But my reference points are this: At 11.30, I established that the firing had stopped. There was a lull. And prior to that, with Minister Rudolf, I had agreed upon a cease-fire. And I received a report from Kozaric, and via him from Zec, and so on. So all this went on until a little after 12.00. So that's the reference point. I can't remember exactly after that because I was constantly having telephone conversations and I was being hurried by General Strugar to come as soon as possible, because I had a conversation with him, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, do you remember -- so on the 6th of December, after Belgrade and Trebinje, what time it was when you arrived at the forward command post in Kupari?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly. It might have been 8.00 or 9.00. I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't need the document any more. Would the usher take it back, please, and provide the witness with the following document, which is P104, Prosecution exhibit. No, I apologise. It's not P104. It is P115, tab 38.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've already seen this document. You saw it during the examination-in-chief. It's the same one, and it was admitted into evidence, tendered by the Prosecution. Could we just go through this document very briefly. Tell me, please, is this a letter written on behalf of the Council for National Defence of Trebinje, and was it signed by its president, Bozidar Vucurevic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the letter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this letter addressed to the Presidency of the SFRY, to the chief of the General Staff in Belgrade, and to the command of the Military Naval Sector in Kumbor and to the 2nd Operative Group command in Trebinje?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The letter is dated the 7th of November. And in the first sentence, it says that the 6th of November was horrid and bloody. So that means that the 6th of November, the previous day, was horrid and bloody. Do you know what it was that happened on the 6th of November? Were there any JNA casualties; dead, wounded?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't think we did have any then. We didn't have any persons who were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the third sentence, it says, in this letter -- or rather, before that, it says that talks are underway between the JNA and the international commission. And then it says: "Around 1330 hours approximately, 200 shells fell on JNA positions. To be more precise, 51 shells on Dubac, 63 on Brgat, and over 100 on Zarkovica." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see where that information of Captain Zarkovic's comes from. The ones that we saw on that document, that's where it comes from, precisely from this document. That is the number of shells that he copied out from here. He did not get it from my operational centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you say who copied it out from who?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do not believe that Vucurevic was at the operations centre. He could never come to my centre in Kupari or Kumbor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So where did Vucurevic get this information from about the exact number of shells? His letter is dated the 7th of November. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know. I don't know. That's why I'm telling you that. That's why I'm so surprised at it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And D54 that we looked at, which gives identical figures concerning the number of shells at Dubac, Brgat, and Zarkovica, that was written on the 6th of November, a day earlier. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And since this document by the assistant commander was written on the 6th of November and sent to Trebinje, Radovici, and Prevlaka, those barracks, could Bozidar Vucurevic get that information about the number of shells fired in the barracks of Trebinje? Could he have received that information there?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he could have. He kept coming to those barracks all the time, and the brigade. He came many more times than I did. That's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Further on it says, in the letter, that on the other side of the front, near the village of Cepikuce, two JNA members, one commander and one soldier, were slaughtered on the other side of the battlefield. Have you heard about that, this incident at Cepikuce?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know about that. I heard about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also it says that while the army is at peace and the participants in the talks offer the frontier to Dubrovnik going from the Old Town, Nuncijata, Lazaret, and Srdj, the Ustashas are firing shells and killing. Are those the enemy positions from which fire was opened at the JNA units? Is that what is referred to in that document written by the assistant commander on the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Further on --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am sorry. It says here in the question "the 6th of December," and what is actually meant is the 6th of November. So it's page 41 -- rather, page 42. And it's line 1. The question should read "the 6th of November," not "the 6th of December."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me, there is a point of objection. The witness has not confirmed that the positions -- that there was fire coming from those particular positions, and I think that that is a misrepresentation of what the evidence is. In other words, particularly going from Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't understand this objection, if the witness said that the information provided by the previous document are identical to the data provided in this letter, in terms of the places from where JNA units were targeted.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: These are two separate questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The objection by Ms. Somers is, at the moment, well-founded, Mr. Rodic, especially when you're trying to identify the situation with respect to the Old Town. I'm not going to suggest a way of you trying to improve it. I think you'll have to try and do that yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, in this letter, is it claimed by Mr. Vucurevic that while the army is at peace and negotiators are offering Dubrovnik a frontier going from the Old Town, Nuncijata, Lazaret and Srdj, Ustashas are firing shells and killing people? Is that what Mr. Vucurevic wrote in this letter?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what he wrote in this letter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In these positions, the Old Town, Nuncijata, Lazaret and Srdj, and he says that that is the positions from which fire is being opened, are these the positions that are also mentioned in the information written by the assistant commander on the 6th of November?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, that's the very point. We have not established that that was written by the assistant commander on the 6th of November. It's what is in the document which is received as Exhibit D54 as apparently a report of the assistant commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I accept that, Your Honour, yes. Let me reformulate my question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this information about the locations from which fire was coming, targeting JNA units, does it correspond to the locations that are listed in Document D54 of the 6th of November 1991?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Furthermore, the letter goes on to state the following, that to the Council for the National Defence of Trebinje, petitions are coming in from JNA units addressed to the council.
