Now, what I want to ask you is this: Is it right that a large number of reservists engaged in the units of the 2nd Operational Group were from Trebinje in actual fact?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Especially in the 472nd Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have already spoken about that, but let me ask you again: Is it true that, inter alia, among the other problems that you highlighted when you spoke about the problems you encountered when commanding during this period of time, that is to say, October to December 1991, that one of the problems was a lack of understanding on the part of the army with respect to the objectives of the operation and why they should take the provocation, why they should remain in one place, why a state of war had not been proclaimed and things along those lines?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did say something about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the basis of your experience and the time spent on that theatre of war, did you pinpoint the overall situation in the country as being a problem, the situation in the SFRY and problems in the Supreme Command of the Yugoslav State Presidency? Did you bring up that as a problem?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the letter, does it say that in these petitions by soldiers, they call for the officers of the reserve force of the JNA to take over the command, who were otherwise on duty in the 2nd Operational Group, because in their opinion lives were being lost in a very banal way? That's what it says?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says. However, that does not reflect the actual situation, the actual state of affairs. This is fanning the flames of an even worse war and attack on Dubrovnik by Mr. Vucurevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that your opinion?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in this letter does it also say that on other fronts in the SFRY, the situation is no better, if not even worse?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, although I can't actually see it here. But I suppose that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The sentence is the following, after mentioning the Old Town, Nuncijata, Lazaret and Srdj, it's in the sentence immediately afterwards. "The information is that the situation is not much better at the other battlefield either or it is even worse."

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, were there many reservists from Trebinje in the 2nd Operational Group? That is to say, in the units of the 2nd Operational Group, and did they lose their lives or were wounded? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know roughly how many soldiers from Trebinje were killed or wounded? What the casualty figures were?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't know that. There is data in the different units. I knew how many there were in the 9th Sector, but I don't have facts and figures about Trebinje, or rather the brigade. I do believe that there may have been most casualties there, the highest number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you informed about the soldiers killed and wounded, the men belonging to units within the composition of the 9th VPS? Would you have been informed about that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was informed -- of course I was, of any of the men killed and wounded within the 9th Sector, although I had information pertaining to the other units of the 2nd Operational Group as well because we received those kinds of reports, all the subordinate commands.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the army informs about who was killed and wounded and sent in a report to the command, do they do their best to supply as much information about those persons as possible, the information that they had available? Would that be true?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, at the end of that letter, are the -- is the top leadership being asked to take measures?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, judging by its contents, does this letter reflect the anxiety and worry of the JNA and the country with respect to the lives of JNA members?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. There's nothing in the letter that represents the JNA at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You're pushing this letter too far again, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, on several occasions the JNA is mentioned in this letter. I do believe that my learned colleague has the document in front of her. You can look at the second sentence, for example --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You're missing my point. You are trying to say this letter is reflecting a view of the JNA. That is the way your question is posed. This is a letter written by one person who had no official role in the JNA. Whether it reflected that person's own personal views is something we can only guess. To say it reflected the views of the whole of the JNA or a large segment of the JNA is something that is beyond the knowledge of the writer of the letter, and no doubt beyond the knowledge of the admiral. So grounding your question in this letter is not going to get you anywhere. If you want to ask the admiral whether there was a general view in the JNA of which he was aware about these things, you might be able to get somewhere that way. But not out of this letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, obviously there's a mistake in the interpretation or translation. I didn't ask it the way it was interpreted. I didn't ask about concern of the JNA, but I asked the witness whether the contents, the contents of this letter reflect the anxieties on the part of the signatory of this letter because this letter was signed by a man outside the JNA. So does it express the concerns of the signatory of this letter for the lives of the members of the JNA, for the country, and so on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The translation is quite the opposite of that. But your own question as you now frame it is simply irrelevant. How is it going to help this Chamber to know what this gentleman was concerned about?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, this letter, does it in any way refer to you personally in view of the addressees?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This letter refers to all the commands of the JNA which were effective in this operation around Dubrovnik. And so this is a direct call to the reservists to replace the incapable and weak traitors and to assume command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which command?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Command over JNA units. That is a direct appeal for them to take over the command by the reserve officers. That's how I understood it. And that is what was attempted in practice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's just clarify matters. When you talk about the appeal to take over the command, whose command? What do you think it refers to?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In concrete terms, my command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you think that this means the takeover of your command by the reservists. But from the heading and title of this letter, one could conclude that it is the reservists who are supposed to take over the role of the Presidency of the SFRY because there is no mention of you personally here in this letter. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, but this is Mr. Rodic's interpretation of something. It is not a real question; it is testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think it's costing us a lot of time, Mr. Rodic, the way you attempt to get established as fact what is expressed in a letter such as this written by one person or in all sorts of reports or orders. We've tried to let you go about your cross-examination because it is your responsibility to conduct the Defence case. But it is a very slow process, and we are achieving comparatively little because you persist in trying to use a letter like this to try to establish facts. Now, the admiral may know certain things. He may know there was a movement to take over his command. He may know that there was an urging on the -- his higher command to replace him by a reservist. He may know things like that. You can ask him about that. But for you to try and say now doesn't this letter mean this and doesn't it mean that, it's only a letter written by one person. It's not going to prove the general facts of this case. I'm trying to show you why there is such difficulty with the way you're approaching this particular line of questioning. What you're ultimately trying to get at may be useful and relevant, but you're battling a very long, hard road because you're trying to get there through a letter like this, or in other cases through various reports or orders. If you think the witness knows relevant information, ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this letter is a Prosecution exhibit - it was introduced and tendered during the examination-in-chief - and the witness has stated his views about the letter. And what he stated was that this letter was an appeal for his replacement, or call for his replacement as commander of the 9th VPS, and that after this letter demonstrations were held by reservists in front of the command and headquarters in Kumbor of the 9th VPS. So if he interpreted the letter in that way in response to a question put to him by the Prosecutor, I really do feel that in the cross-examination itself, bearing in mind the contents of the letter itself, the Defence would have the right to ask how he came by that conclusion, how he deduced that. That is to say, the witness relying on the contents of the letter alone, because the witness, during the examination-in-chief, did not provide us with any further information except for the kind you have mentioned now, whether he had any other knowledge or information, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, if you have the view that the matters that you've just put to us were the effect of the witness in evidence in chief, what more are you seeking to gain? Isn't that what you want?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I just wanted to check it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, it got there in evidence in chief. And now we've spent about a quarter of an hour, and you're trying to get back to where the Prosecution got to. If it's there and it's good, there's no need to go back over it. If you think it's wrong, by all means.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, just to make the record straight: The Prosecution tendered this document for a very different reason. And I know that the Chamber realises that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We are aware that your use of the document was different. But I think there's also much in what Mr. Rodic has said about the evidence given by the witness about it. And that's one of the reasons why I can't understand, frankly, why so much time is being spent.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour. Obviously there is a misunderstanding in this regard. Then I'm going to move on to other matters. In relation to this witness, I would just like to ask one more thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Bearing in mind this letter and the time when you were commander of the 9th VPS in 1991, and if you look at the events in the territory where you were and your knowledge regarding the situation in the entire country, were there any similar or even more serious speeches and actions in public by soldiers, politicians, public figures, and so on?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I have to object, Your Honour. This calls for a value judgement that simply is not an appropriate question based on the line -- based on the issues that are raised with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think there are sufficient reason and foundation for the question being put. It's being put as a matter of general knowledge. Carry on, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, could you please give me an answer. If you remember the question, that is.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember the question, of course. I would like to say that this certainly was not the only example of public speech or action along these lines; that is to say, along the lines of Mr. Vucurevic's thinking. There were such actions or speeches from the lowest level up to the highest level. Attacks on the JNA calls for intransigence, calls for an energetic dealing with the opposite side. And in all these documents and similar statements, there is no reference to resolving the crisis by peaceful means. I could mention a great many examples, similar, nationalist, extremist ones, coming from both sides, our side and the opposite side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We know that there was a great deal of that. But tell me, from the superior commands of the 2nd Operational Group of the General Staff and the Federal Secretary for National Defence, were you replaced? Were you removed by them after this letter?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I hear of any such thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Even after this letter, did you and other JNA commanders try to resolve the issue of disarming paramilitaries in Dubrovnik by peaceful means?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the usher to have this document distributed, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I would like to interrupt you there. As we rather had taken you out of your line of thinking, I think it's probably a convenient time to raise with you the question of how you see the course of your cross-examination and how much longer you would expect to be. By the end of today, you will have cross-examined for some five days. And that's a very long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I address the issue after the break, Your Honour, after I check this out, exactly how long I spent cross-examining?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Don't worry about how long you have spent. We're concerned about how long you would like to spend in the future, Mr. Rodic. The information I have is that you had all but some 40 minutes on the 1st of April, you had all of the 2nd of April, the 5th of April, the 13th of April, and now today, the 14th. Now that's the past. Don't worry about that. Your cross-examination has exceeded the length of the examination already. Our concern is to learn about the future. And certainly, we will break a little early now and give you time to think about that, because as we have indicated in the past, although we are trying to give you a free hand, we can't let time just continue to run on. And I think the point has been reached in this cross-examination where that has got to be some very careful control of time. So we'll allow you to think about that over a break and hear from you when we return.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before the break, I promised to give you an answer after the break in relation to the length of cross-examination. The Defence wishes to emphasise first and foremost, and I think that the Trial Chamber is fully aware of that, too, that this is a very important witness, both for the Prosecution and for the Defence. Perhaps even more so for the Defence because this is the only witness from the JNA who held a high position and who was also together with the accused person. This witness was interviewed in July 2002, September 2003, and September 2004, and in April, not to mention the situation from March and April this year. You know how all that material was provided to the Defence; without a transcript. Also, I wish to note that when announcing this witness, the Prosecution said that the examination-in-chief would last for three days. However, they went beyond their original estimate, too. Their examination-in-chief went on for five days, minus 40 minutes. And that is when I started my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think it's four days and 36 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can remember, it was the 24th, 25th, 26th, and 29th of March, and then on the 1st of April two sessions. But at any rate, it went beyond the original estimate. I understand that, because there is an enormous number of documents involved, and also the period about which the witness is testifying is a lengthy one and involving many different events. Then also the cross-examination has taken quite a while because the witness pauses considerably. Before starting his answer, he is waiting for the transcript to end, the typing to end, and then he starts giving an answer. Also while he was testifying, he waits for every word he says to be recorded in the transcript, and then he proceeds. There are 42 exhibits that were proffered by the Prosecution. That is a large number of documents. And the Defence has already tendered about ten documents. We have at least about 20 other important documents that we wish to tender through the cross-examination. Then also for this witness and for the Defence, there are relevant exhibits that were introduced by the Prosecution in the proceedings to date. I am particularly referring to the exhibits introduced through the European Mission, including Witness Hvalkof. The Defence has to deal with that, those exhibits and that binder. At any rate, bearing all of this in mind, I'm aware that the examination could take much longer than the Defence had originally planned. Of course, bearing in mind how precious time is, but in view of everything I said, the assessment of the Defence is that we could finish the cross-examination on Monday. Of course, bearing in mind that this should deal with the most substantive matters that are relevant to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, we are very well aware of the matters that you have mentioned. Partly for that reason, we have been silent these five days on the topic. But the idea that you would want after today yet a further three days, producing a total of some eight days, seems to us to be unnecessarily long. The significant issue that you omitted from your description of things was the degree of time that you have spent over certain matters which are not perhaps of first-rank importance in the case. So that if you were now to look at all the material you have and to ask yourself the question which of those matters are really of significance to the Defence, I would think it would be possible for you to reduce your estimate. The view of the Chamber is that we ought to be able to conclude the evidence of this witness this week. That will give you from now two more full days, and then we'll allow a little time for re-examination. So if you could from this point on bear that in mind, we would be grateful. And there will be this session now, but you'll have an opportunity overnight to look more closely at the material you have of potential questioning, and I think be able to refine that down. In light of the experience so far, there will be some matters I suspect you'll be able to put aside. So our requirement, then, Mr. Rodic, is that the evidence of the present witness should be concluded this week, including re-examination. Thank you very much. Perhaps you'd better get moving.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I shall do my best.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, as far as promotion is concerned, promotions in the Yugoslav People's Army, there is a regular procedure and there is an exceptional procedure. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me approximately how long the procedure lasts when exceptional promotion is involved?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. There are regulations, peacetime regulations, and this is not really regulated, but in peacetime, again, a procedure has to be carried out, just like with regular promotions. That is to say that when a unit is putting forth such a proposal, it sends it to the higher instance. All proposals are compiled in the command of the army, which is the highest instance, and then they send this on to the personnel administration of the JNA. And it is the personnel administration that actually carries out the promotions. However, it can be a shorter procedure as well. It depends. If there are exceptional circumstances involved. As a matter of fact, this is rather flexible, so a commander of a certain rank can shorten the procedure involved. It all depends on a particular individual, a particular event, why a person is being promoted exceptionally, why there is early promotion, what are the merits involved, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As for the exceptional promotion of Vladimir Kovacevic, you said that it was his own unit that he hailed from that was in charge of that promotion. And it was above the 3rd Battalion, the superior unit, and that was the 472nd Motorised Brigade and that it was the only one that could have put forth the proposal for early promotion. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I think, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree that the proposal for the exceptional promotion of Vladimir Kovacevic, bearing in mind the date of the 11th of November 1991, has to do with his merits pertaining to combat activities that took place in that period and that that could have to do with the taking of Bosanka?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it does not have to do with Bosanka. On the 11th of November, Bosanka was not taken. Bosanka was taken on the 9th, between the 8th and 9th of November, that is, and he did not take part in that attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he have any activities on the 11th of November on account of which he could have been nominated for exceptional promotion, because that is the date that figures in the exceptional promotion.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 11th of November and on the 12th of November, that unit, his unit, Captain Kovacevic's unit, participated in the taking of the forts of Gradci and Strincijera. Probably - of course I didn't know it then - but probably that was the occasion on account of which he was nominated for promotion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the 9th VPS, as the superior command of the 472nd Motorised Brigade in that period, did it send further on this proposal for exceptional promotion to the 2nd Operational Group and they then further on to the General Staff and the personnel administration of the Federal Secretariat for National Defence?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the answer is no. I investigated who it was who sent this proposal, and I asked the organs of the 9th Sector and the organs of the personnel administration of the JNA, General Branko Fezer, and I could not establish any facts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me what it was that you could not establish.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not establish who sent in the proposal, where the original idea came from, and who gave a positive assessment, and the road the proposal took until it reached the personnel department. I wasn't able to establish that. I was told that the proposals are not stored but are destroyed with that year of promotion, when it expires. That's the standard procedure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Otherwise the regular procedure, is it that the superior commands send on one to the other, or rather the subordinate to the superior, up the chain of command until it reaches the top-most level in the chain?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the regular procedure. However, in this particular case, I cannot know when the proposal was sent out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask the usher's assistance again, please, and have the witness shown a document. It is Exhibit P61, Prosecution Exhibit 61, tab 26.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a letter, Mr. Jokic, sent by Minister Kouchner to the head of the Monitoring Mission, the Dutch ambassador, and the date is the 23rd of November --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I believe that is not what was referred to as P61, tab 26. Perhaps we could get that clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The document I have at tab 26 is quite different from that, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in tab 26, which I received from the Prosecution, is a letter from Minister Kouchner dated the 23rd of November sent to the head of mission. And the previous document from tab 26 is a letter by the head of mission addressed to Minister Kouchner. Perhaps there's a mix-up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You must have a different binder, not the binder that was used in respect of the present witness, if you're going back to Exhibit P61.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, P61 on the list is the binder for Witness Hvalkof, and there are 42 tabs there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We have the document identified now. It doesn't help us greatly as we don't have it with us. But carry on, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: May I respectfully ask that it go on the ELMO, if you have it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, on the 23rd of November, or before that, did you meet Minister Kouchner at all? Because here in his letter, he says that "Negotiations are now on the federal side at the level of General Damjanovic and Admiral Jokic."

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all. What I said was that I met him in Mokosica, and that's all, that the negotiations were conducted by Colonel Damjanovic on that occasion, and he was promoted that very day to the rank of general. And that was the 21st of November. And after that, I did not conduct any negotiations whatsoever, nor did I take part in any. And I didn't then either except that we agreed that we would enter into Mokosica peacefully.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, is this quotation from Mr. Kouchner's letter addressed to the head of mission incorrect in which you are mentioned as one of the negotiators on behalf of the Federation?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps he considered that I took part in the negotiations on the 21st. I don't know where he came from at all. He came from Dubrovnik, and he was brought in by Damjanovic. So it's clear who led the negotiations then. And he's mentioned here first. He's the first name mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why does Minister Kouchner mention you, too?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he probably thought that since we were in Mokosica together and led negotiations about the surrender of weapons in Mokosica, that I was included in the negotiations. But, if you want me to, I can tell you who he negotiated with later on, where that took place, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's no need. Just tell me, when were you together with him? Was it the 21st of November?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, just that one time in Mokosica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I have the usher's assistance again, please. And from P61, the same exhibit, show the document from tab 28.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On Monday, the 25th of November, did you, as it says here, the military and navy commanders of the JNA in the Dubrovnik area, General Damjanovic and Admiral Jokic, on the JNA side take part in this agreement with the mayor of Dubrovnik, Mr. Pero Poljanic, and the commander of the Croatian army in the Dubrovnik area, Nikola Obuljen, on the Croatian side in the presence of Mr. B. Kouchner, agreed on these three points as they are set out to follow.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. This is the first time I see this document. And as for Dubrovnik, I wasn't in Dubrovnik during the operation at all, nor do I have any idea of what this is all about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, why, then, in the memorandum of the agreement would your name be specified? Do you have any information about that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have no information about that. But I think that this document is nonsensical as far as my name is concerned and my stay in Dubrovnik. That is the face of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So with respect to you personally, everything mentioned in this document is not true?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Tell me, please --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Or rather, I'd like to ask the usher's assistance again. Would he show the witness another document. It's P61, from tab 29.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, this is a report sent by the deputy head of the regional centre of Dubrovnik; that is to say, from the Monitoring Mission for his operational group in the regional centre of Split. And the subject is the meeting between Minister Rudolf and yourself in Cavtat from 1000 to 1300 hours in December 1991. 1st of December 1991. You were at that meeting, were you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that this meeting was held, as it says, in a friendly and positive atmosphere, as Mr. Rudolf says?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely correct. I remember this very well, and I even proposed that the talk should be held without them, but not with a view to excluding them. I didn't say without them. What I meant was there should be no translation, no interpretation, so that we could work as efficiently as possible and reach an agreement as soon as possible. So that was the gist of my proposal and why I proposed it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please now take a look at paragraph 3 where it says that Mr. Rudolf said that the following topics were discussed: A, B, C, D, and E. Was that how it was? Was that what happened?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't quite like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to 3A.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An unconditional cease-fire was accepted independently of the fact that the agreement had not been signed. So all these points were accepted, were agreed upon, except the control of ships, and it remained to be seen whether this check should be done at sea or in the ports. That was the only point challenged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you mean 3D?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And we were supposed to rule on that the next day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As it is written down here, was the proposal, or your proposal on the 5th of December that the officers of the JNA in civilian clothes should control the cargo in the port along with supervision by the European Community?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which harbour did this refer to?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Dubrovnik harbour, the port of Gruz.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what on the 5th of December did the Croatian side think with respect to that matter? Or rather, what were their proposals or demands on the subject?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They demanded that the ships be controlled and checked in the port of Gruz. And I wasn't able to accept that at that time in view of the security problems for that team of officers. So that was the only reason why the agreement wasn't signed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the letter that we looked at a moment ago, dated the 6th of December that you sent to Minister Rudolf, under item 4, point 4, you proposed that the vessels be controlled in the port of Gruz. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. When I concluded the negotiations in Cavtat on the 5th of December, I went to the command post of the 2nd Operational Group and informed General Strugar about the talks that were held. And I happened to mention this matter of the control and check of ships. And he -- actually, he didn't mind whether it was done at sea or on land. What he said, the important thing was that the ships should be checked and controlled. Whether it was done at sea or in the port was immaterial. And I took that to mean that that item should not be cause for not signing the agreement, should not be a reason why the agreement was not signed, so I accepted the port of Gruz as being the location.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why didn't you accept it straight away on the 5th of December?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already told you why; because there were several officers who would have to do the actual work. And in a hostile environment, in an environment which could have erupted in incidents at any moment because the captain of the frigate, Jeremic, had already informed me, and he had been to Dubrovnik several times, that he was almost attacked by the citizens and by persons in uniform as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in the proposal from the Dubrovnik side on the 5th of December to carry out this control in the port of Gruz, along with the presence of the EC Monitoring Mission, did the Croatian side on that occasion, the 5th of December, guarantee the security and safety of the JNA officers who would conduct that check and control of the vessels?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, of course, they did. They guaranteed the same thing to Jeremic and all the others who entered town. It is only natural for them to give such guarantees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If they gave such guarantees on the 5th of December, too, then there was no reason for that kind of concern. Could this agreement not have been accepted on the 5th?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, now. If that is the way you put it now, it seems only natural. However, one had to be there then at the time, and then one would realise how well-founded my concern for my officers was at the time. Because there had been casualties in that port of Gruz. There were casualties among the civilians as well. It was hard to prevent the incidents that could have occurred and in which these officers would have been the target.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the usher for his assistance to place tab 30 from P61 before the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, this is a log sheet of one of the members of the ECMM mission in Dubrovnik, Mr. Per Hvalkof, who was there at the time. Do you know him from the negotiations of the 5th and 7th of December, the negotiations you had with the Dubrovnik side? Because on the 7th of December, he verified the agreement that you had reached.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please look at page 1. The time is 0600 hours. It's the log sheet for the 6th of December. It says: "Shelling from land and sea towards the fortress close to the TV tower, Sroj - it's actually supposed to be Srdj - and the harbour commenced." And then on the right-hand side there are remarks saying that Split and Zagreb had already been informed about it. Was there any shelling from land and sea against Srdj on the morning of the 6th at 6.00?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no information regarding the shelling coming from the sea. But from land, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you investigate whether there had been any operations from the sea on the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you establish that there weren't any operations from sea?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I established.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this incorrect information, then, from this log sheet where it says that at 6.00 in the morning on the 6th of December there was shelling from sea as well?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely incorrect. We looked at all the ship logbooks from two ships that were at sea at that time. The commander of the defence of the town of Dubrovnik also says that, according to his information, on the 6th the ships did not take any action.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which commander said that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Nojko Marinovic, commander of the defence of the town of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you read this?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In his testimony, in his statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this testimony given before this Tribunal? Was this statement made to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's right. But what I'm saying is that we checked the ship logbooks for the 6th of December.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, look at the time of 0920 hours where it says that Minister Rudolf talked to the secretary of Admiral Jokic that a cease-fire had been promised and meeting agreed upon for 11.00 at Cavtat. Can you tell us something about this particular remark.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that my secretary's name is Ivan Hrvoje.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters' note that the question used the feminine form in B/C/S, and the name is a masculine one.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he actually spoke to them. Maybe he said that he knew where I was or he didn't know where I was, but since he is a noncommissioned officer, I don't know what he could have said and how he could have made any promises regarding a cease-fire. That is not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But is it possible that on the 6th of December, when you left Kumbor, this alleged lady secretary of yours, and you say that it's an NCO, was not in Cavtat at all, that he was not in Cavtat at all?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he was not. He was in Kumbor in the office, or rather in the operations centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know anything about this particular remark, that at 0920, someone was talked to, some person who was your secretary, male or female, and regarding this meeting in Cavtat, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I talked to Minister Rudolf sometime between 9.00 and 10.00, or rather, I spoke to him twice. During the first conversation, he claimed to me that the Old Town was being attacked and I said to him that that was not correct, that our unit was targeting Srdj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, can you remember at what time this first conversation took place?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was around 10.00, between 9.30 and 10.00, because I was in Cavtat, I think. I was supposed to be there, judging by everything, because I carried out the second conversation from Cavtat because that's when he told me, "Can't you hear the shells falling on the Old Town?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Could you please look at the time of 10 past 11.00 in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask for the paper on the ELMO to be moved so that the Trial Chamber can see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It says here that there was a message from the naval base in Boka Kotorska that the JNA would cease-fire at 11.15. Who was it that conveyed this message as is stated here and that a meeting was planned for Cavtat for 1330 hours? Is the content of this remark correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not sure because it was not possible for this meeting, but the cease-fire I'm sure about that, yes. As for 11.15, I think that we agreed on 11.00 or 11.30. But if he wrote 11.15, then it's possible. And that is what I reported. That is what I informed Minister Rudolf of and Kozaric also, informing him to tell Zec. And that's the way it was, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, around 7.00 in the morning on the 6th of December, did you receive any kind of fax, a fax message from the Dubrovnik side or from the crisis staff or from the Monitoring Mission?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. I have no recollection of that. I think the answer is no. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please take a look at 1430 hours. The message received by Minister Rudolf is referred to here. Please read it and see whether it corresponds to your message of the 6th of December. And you said that you dictated that message to Captain Kurdulija.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are just some elements -- well, possibly. But I'm surprised that there are only two or three things from that message that are referred to. Yes, well, since this was a translation, then yes, it's possible. The time is approximately the right one, 1430.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please look at 1531. It says that a copy of the message received from Captain Jokic was translated.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, you certainly were not in Cavtat.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I wasn't. That is right. It could be right in terms of the time involved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And please look at 1610. It says: "Minister Rudolf informs me - Mr. Hvalkof - that General Strugar has now ordered immediate cease-fire." At that time, could Minister Rudolf have spoken to General Strugar at all?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Perhaps with his headquarters, but not him because General Strugar was with me in Belgrade at the time. Probably his chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please ask the usher to place before the witness tab 31. From Exhibit P61, that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the introduction, you have it in Serbian, and I should like the usher to place a copy -- but we only have one copy. Could that one copy be placed on the ELMO, then, please. Mr. Jokic, this was signed by Per Hvalkof, the man you met at these negotiations. And he says that he sent a fax to your name from the ECMM on the 6th of December, and that the fax, at 7.12 hours in the morning, was sent to the VPS at Boka. Did you receive a fax like that, this message? Were you informed of that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably the fax did arrive. I think that between 7.00 and 8.00, or 8.30, I had at least 30 telephone conversations back and forth between me and Kupari and Trebinje, Podgorica, and so on. So probably it arrived during that period of time. If that's what it says, then probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean, "If that's what it says"?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember because all these other events were taking place at the same time, everything that this fax refers to. I was solving those questions and I was engaged in doing that. So as I say, I can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But why a moment ago when I showed you the log sheet by Mr. Hvalkof with the times listed and when I asked whether at around 7.00 a.m. you received a fax from the Monitoring Mission, your answer was that you did not, you had not? Was it because it wasn't recorded in the log sheet that a fax had been sent to you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm saying now that I can't remember that at all. I am not denying that it arrived. What I'm saying is that I can't even remember to this day that it arrived. Probably it did. But as I say, at that time I was busy doing -- engaged in other matters. And I invested my efforts to stop the attack. Between 6.00 and 8.00, that was the only thing that I was doing. I was interested in nothing else but achieving that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you now take a look at the second half written in English. On the left-hand side, you have the signature of Mr. Hvalkof; on the right-hand side, it has -- it says "Sent 060714, Nov. - abbreviation - 1991." Do you have any comments to make with respect to that entry?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know. I don't know what it means.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could that be November 1991?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says. But I don't know what this 060714 means. I don't know what that means.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me, since at the time in the morning you were still in Kumbor, is it possible that nobody of your subordinate officers would not have handed you this fax or informed you about it? Would that be possible?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it would not be possible. Had it arrived at headquarters and not been handed over to me, that is quite impossible, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness now be shown a document from tab 32, also within Exhibit P61.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Take a look at the upper left-hand corner. The abbreviation "ORS Dubrovnik," is that the coastal radar station of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you -- this radiogram sent to the VPS of Boka, did you receive it that morning? That is to say, the 6th of December 1991, because it says "urgent," "urgently forward," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, although I don't remember. What I do know is --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Jokic, let's do our best to be as precise as possible and try to avoid answers like "probably," "I think," "I assume," and so on. Did you receive this message?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said, sir, that I do not remember. I knew that there were operations against Srdj at this time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time was that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So 0550 hours, you had information that the JNA had opened fire on Srdj?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I said I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But there's mention here of opening fire from -- ship artillery fire on Dubrovnik, which means that the crisis staff of Dubrovnik for that time period is warning the command of the VPS of Boka that there was firing from ship artillery on Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no ship artillery fire at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is this an incorrect piece of information once again?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me, please, how, then, this document was not shown you either, like the previous fax.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that it was not shown to me. I didn't tell you that. I didn't say that the document wasn't shown.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But do you remember that on the 6th in the morning -- do you remember having read it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I do not remember the document. I did not say that it was not. I said that I did not remember it because if somebody brought this document in to me at that time, I was busy trying to stop a willful attack on the part of Captain Kovacevic, and all the lines were down at the time so nobody could reach me. The chief of the General Staff couldn't, or General Kadijevic or Admiral Kandic or General Strugar, who were probably all ringing me up and trying to reach me. And that's a fact. That's how things stood, and this situation went on for at least an hour while I was on relay communication.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, would that be a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rodic, it would be. We will resume tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
